content.intro: This lesson focuses on troubleshooting runners and networking. Runner/network failures require checking runner state, tool availability, DNS, permissions, ports, registry connectivity, and safe access to private services. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Runner/network failures require checking runner state, tool availability, DNS, permissions, ports, registry connectivity, and safe access to private services. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Jobs stuck in queues
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Offline self-hosted runners
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Missing software
items.text: For missing software, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Permission and file-system errors
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: DNS and connectivity issues
items.text: For dns and connectivity issues, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Registry and external service connectivity
items.text: Build and identify an image deterministically, grant only required registry permissions, scan/verify before promotion, and prefer immutable digests or traceable tags over mutable “latest” references.

content_blocks.code:
name: Check configured endpoint
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  healthcheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Request health endpoint
        env:
          HEALTHCHECK_URL: ${{ vars.HEALTHCHECK_URL }}
        run: curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 10 "$HEALTHCHECK_URL"
content_blocks.expected_output: The step succeeds for a successful HTTP response and times out after ten seconds; a configured endpoint is required.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test endpoint that the runner is allowed to reach and check the URL variable before running.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not put passwords or tokens in the URL variable or echo full authenticated URLs.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to troubleshooting runners and networking. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain troubleshooting runners and networking, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Turn run status, logs, and diagnostic data into a systematic troubleshooting process.

content.task: Apply troubleshooting runners and networking to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Runner/network failures require checking runner state, tool availability, DNS, permissions, ports, registry connectivity, and safe access to private services. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Runner/network failures require checking runner state, tool availability, DNS, permissions, ports, registry connectivity, and safe access to private services.

Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.
